How I test

Every test run ends in a report a developer can act on without asking me a single question. This is the format I use, with a real excerpt.

  1. Set the scope

    App, environment, role, the exact flow under test, method, and the test data I created, all written down before I start.

  2. Write cases per role

    Each case gets an ID, the scenario, the expected result, the actual result, and a verdict: pass, fail, or pass with notes.

  3. Hunt the edge cases

    Empty fields, invalid input, inconsistent totals, simulated payment failures, overlapping geometry, duplicates.

  4. Report bugs to reproduce

    Severity, where it happens, steps, expected versus actual. No vague “it doesn’t work”.

  5. Retest and close

    A checklist of what wasn’t covered yet, and every bug retested after the fix.

Clear rules for messy data

For polygon uploads, I agreed three outcomes with the team before testing, then updated the expected results to match how the platform really behaved.

Pass

Overlap below the digitising tolerance.

  • Tiny edge overlap between neighbouring plots
  • Same geometry uploaded in separate, sequential files

Flag

Significant partial overlap, sent for human review.

  • Partial overlap inside one bill of lading
  • A sliver of about 0.0126% over protected forest

Reject

Full containment or a duplicate.

  • MultiPolygon upload, since only Polygon is accepted
  • Duplicate geometry inside the same file

How I design a system

Before any screen, I pin down who does what, which states data moves through, and what is still undecided. Here’s my method on a made-up example.

example case, made up for this page

KopiLot: tracing a coffee lot from farm to cup

A farmer group sends green coffee to a washing station, an inspector grades each lot, an exporter ships it, and any buyer can scan a QR code to see where the beans came from.

Swimlanes across every actor

One picture of the whole process, so every party sees where it hands work to the next.

States, not just screens

Every status change has a trigger and an owner, so testers know exactly what to check.

StatusTriggered byWho
DraftLot savedWashing station
Awaiting gradingGrading requestedWashing station
SampledSample loggedInspector
Needs revisionData doesn’t match sampleInspector
ApprovedGrade signed offInspector
ShippedShipment bookedExporter

One decision gate, with a way back

Only the inspector can approve a grade, and a failed check goes back to the washing station instead of dead-ending.

Integrations as contracts

The lab’s cupping system talks to the platform through three agreed calls.

POST /lots farm, weight_kg → lot_id POST /lots/{id}/grades cupping_score → grade + status GET /public/lots/{qr} → origin, grade, route

Data models that survive edge cases

When lots are blended, each source keeps its share by weight, and the shares always add up to 100%.

wi = mi ÷ Σm

FarmLot per farm + harvestBlend of lotsShipment

Open questions stay visible

Nothing gets decided silently. Each open point gets a code until the client answers.

  • OQ-01Can a farmer group appeal a grade?
  • OQ-02What happens to the QR if a lot ships in two parts?
  • OQ-03Who can void a published QR code?

Sources you can edit

Diagrams come with their source, Mermaid or draw.io XML generated by Python, so the team can update them without me. Documents are split by job: PRD, user stories, and checklists live apart.
